title: Not as those without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beatific vision: Moses hidden in the rock, and Paul's hope, then face to face. Your line was face to face. Who got your full attention? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-nine.

Two words in the King James Bible: "Jesus wept." He has just asked where they laid his friend Lazarus, and they've answered, come and see. In John's telling he is about to call Lazarus out of the grave. He weeps anyway. Keep those two words close, because today's line comes from Paul, writing to a young church in Thessalonica that had buried some of its own. This block met his sentence once already, read for what it says about the end. Today we read it for what it says about grief. It's easy to hear it as an order to stop crying. Read slowly, it says something else, and its last words are today's word.

Here's the sentence, in the King James words: "But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope." First, read it slowly, because it's easy to misread. Paul doesn't say: don't sorrow. He says: don't sorrow even as, the same way as, those with no hope. Grief is assumed. He never asks them to stop crying. He asks what their tears are leaning on. Paul doesn't describe anyone else's grief; his attention is on the church he's writing to. Second, the word asleep. Paul calls the dead them which are asleep. It's gentle, and it carries a hope inside it, because sleep is something you wake from. He goes on: "For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him." Third, back to Lazarus. In John's story, Jesus weeps knowing what he is about to do. The hope doesn't cancel the tears. It stands next to them. That's the shape Paul is asking for: tears, with something underneath them. Fourth, grief kept company. Paul tells the church in Rome, "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." Not explain to them. Not hurry them along. Weep with them. Christian grief, in these letters, is not quieter or tidier than anyone's. It cries, and it doesn't cry alone.

Here's the practice: grieve, with hope. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a loss: a person, or something else you've had to let go of. Let yourself feel its weight. Don't hurry past it. Then, if you pray, you can hold it alongside Paul's words: them which are asleep. If you don't pray, you can hold it alongside one good thing that loss left in you, a habit, a laugh, a way of seeing. Let the grief and the hope sit next to each other without either one winning. The bell holds the time.
Not as those without hope. Paul's phrase in First Thessalonians four: Christians grieve, and their grief leans on the hope of the resurrection.

howItsDone: 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 is among the readings offered in some churches' funeral services, and some Christians speak of the dead as having fallen asleep in Christ.

match.prompt: not as those without hope — tap the pairs.
pairs: on the way to Lazarus's grave

myth: Paul tells the Thessalonians not to grieve
he says don't sorrow "even as others which have no hope." grief is assumed.
Jesus wept on his way to Lazarus's grave
"Jesus wept," though in the story he was about to raise his friend. he reaches the grave three verses later.
Paul tells the Romans to cheer up those who weep
"weep with them that weep." he asks for company in grief, not a quick fix.

fork.setup: you're Paul. a young church writes that some of their own have died, and they're grieving and afraid. what's the first thing you say about their dead?
options: stop crying; it shows weak faith.
grieve, but not like those with no hope.
don't think about it; focus on the living.
fork.reveal: "that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope." he doesn't forbid grief. he tells them what it can lean on.

original.note: Greek: those who are sleeping, Paul's word for the dead in 1 Thessalonians 4:13. from the same verb comes koimētērion, a sleeping place: cemetery.

trapdoor: what you thought: Christians are told not to be sad when someone dies.
what it means: Paul assumes they grieve, and asks them to grieve leaning on hope, and to weep with those who weep.
what a scholar hears: the weight falls on 'even as': sorrow not even as others. and the dead are 'asleep', a word that expects a waking.
recall: the first and last Greek letters

notes: Angle chosen to avoid day 1316 (rapture; 'ever with the Lord'): today stays with 4:13–14, 18 and grief.
Hook: the situation in Thessalonica (deaths in the community; worry about the dead) is inferred from the letter, and the script says 'suggests'.
'Others which have no hope' is left undescribed on purpose, so no group becomes a foil. Confirm.
howItsDone: confirm 1 Thessalonians 4 appears among funeral readings (e.g., Catholic Order of Christian Funerals).
Original: ἐλπίς; in 4:13 the phrase is μὴ ἔχοντες ἐλπίδα. Confirm.

Audit pass (2026-10-02): match pair and myth placed "Jesus wept" at the tomb; John 11:35 has him weeping after "come and see", before he "cometh to the grave" (11:38); fixed.
